title: Meet Corvane: One Company at Five Sizes

The journal spec gives a front-matter page no thesis, so the thesis here was written for this spec; its agreement with the journal spec was not checked by the journal-spec process, and it was written to argue the Preface's supporting claim PF-3.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page can list Corvane's five stages in order with the approximate headcount and the main incident of each.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: list Corvane's five stages, the rough headcount at each, and one thing that broke.
acceptance_criteria.expected: Five stages near 12, 50, 150, 500 and 1,100 people, each with its named incident.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The page states in its first paragraph that Corvane is fictional, and no figure on it is presented as data about a real company.

thesis.question: Which company do the book's examples come from, and what happens to it as it grows?
thesis.claim: The book's examples come from Corvane, a fictional field-service scheduling software company followed from 12 to about 1,100 people in five stages. At each stage its structure was a reasonable answer to the problem in front of the company when it was built, and its named incidents happened where growth had since made a different capacity scarce and the structure had stayed as it was, so each incident is an instance of a failure pattern and none of them needed a careless person.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a growing company's troubles are growing pains: particular to its people and its moment, to be expected, and explained well enough by who was in charge when they happened.
thesis.so_what: A reader who accepts this reads every Corvane scene in a later chapter by asking what the structure was built for and what had become scarce since, and can place the scene on one timeline instead of meeting it as an anecdote.
thesis.how_why: Growth changes which of attention, judgment and verification runs out first, while the structure built around the earlier shortage stays in place; what the old structure then produces is a queue, a duplicate or a decision made without its information, whoever holds the roles. One invented company with fixed facts shows the same thing happening five times.

supporting_claims.claim: Corvane is fictional and makes one product whose parts are built by different teams and must agree with each other, so a gap between teams reaches customers as a visible fault.

In each of five stages, from 12 to about 1,100 people, the structure answered the problem in front of the company when it was built, and the stage's named incident came where growth had made a different capacity scarce and the structure had stayed.
The same small cast of roles is present through the stages, and no incident is explained by the failing of one of them.
Each named incident is an instance of one of the twelve failure patterns, and between them the cases touch all four families, the incentives family only as a risk.
Because the stages, people and incidents are fixed in one record, a later chapter can cite any of them in a phrase and the reader can look it up here.

role.contribution: Introduces the running example and its timeline, so that later chapters can cite a stage or incident in one phrase.

additional_patterns.applies_to: five-stages: the five stages in the order Corvane lived them, 2018 to 2028

flow.rationale: Each section supplies what the next one refers to. The product comes first because every incident is a fault in that product or in the flow that ships it. The stages come before the cast because a role only means something at a size (a VP Engineering who joins in 2023 joins a company of a known shape). The cast comes before the incident table because the table is free of names only if the reader has already been told that the people are roles and not culprits. The incidents are mapped to patterns only after each has been told in its stage, so the table classifies things the reader has already met. The usage table is last because it is a lookup, used after reading and from later chapters. Putting the pattern table first would classify incidents not yet told; putting the usage table first would list chapters against names that mean nothing yet.

hook.content: The previous page named twelve ways a product and tech organization fails. This page gives one company in which those failures happen in turn as it grows: Corvane, which is fictional.

bridge.from_reader_world: The reader has just met twelve failure patterns as names with mechanisms, and has seen Corvane only as the puzzle in the introduction: a company that doubled its engineers and shipped less.
bridge.to_topic: The page gives that company whole and once, an invented company with fixed facts, so that every later chapter can cite a stage or an incident in a phrase.

thesis_statement.text: At each of five sizes Corvane's structure was a reasonable answer to the problem in front of the company when it was built, and each named incident happened where growth had since made something else scarce and the structure had stayed; none of the incidents needed a careless person.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout (second bullet) and the second lead paragraph (p02)

sections.heading: Corvane and Its Product
sections.controlling_idea: Corvane makes one product in three parts that must agree with each other, which is why its organizational faults reach customers where they can be seen.

advances_thesis.how: Describes the company and says why this product makes structural faults visible.

transition_in.carries_over: The promise to give the company whole.
transition_in.introduces: What the company makes and for whom.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Corvane, founded in Rotterdam in 2018, sells scheduling and dispatch software to field-service companies as an office application for planners, a mobile app for technicians and integrations with customers' billing and stock systems, paid per technician per month.

evidence.what: The company paragraph of the ledger: product, three parts, customers (heating, lifts, telecom installation), pricing, founding year and city.
evidence.shows: Fixes the product every incident is a fault in.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The product suits the book because one scheduling rule has to hold in all three parts, so when the teams that build the parts disagree, a planner and a technician see the disagreement the same day.

evidence.what: A job assigned in the office application must appear on the technician's phone and later in the customer's billing export; a rule about overlapping jobs or job status that differs between parts shows up as two schedules or an unbilled job.
evidence.shows: Explains why Corvane's organizational faults can be shown as product faults, without telling an incident before its stage.

transition_in.introduces: Why that makes gaps between teams visible to customers.

sections.heading: Five Stages, 2018 to 2028
sections.controlling_idea: Corvane passes through five stages, from 12 to about 1,100 people, and in each the structure answers the problem of its moment and the named incident arrives where a different capacity has become scarce.

advances_thesis.how: Tells each stage with its size, structure, scarce capacity and incident, then states what the five have in common.

flow.rationale: The stages are told in the order they happened because each stage's structure is the answer to the stage before it; the summary figure and table come first so the reader has the whole timeline before the detail, and the common shape is stated last because it is a claim about all five.

transition_in.introduces: What happens to the company as it grows, stage by stage.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each stage is read by which of three capacities is running short: attention (how much a team can hold in mind well enough to change it safely), judgment (deciding with the relevant information at hand) and verification (knowing that what was built is right).

evidence.what: The one-clause definitions of the three capacities used in chapter 1 of this book.
evidence.shows: Defines the terms of the table's 'scarce capacity' column before the table uses them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The five stages run from one team of 12 people in 2018 to two business units of about 1,100 in 2028, and each ends in an incident Corvane's people gave a name.

evidence.what: Mermaid flowchart, left to right: five nodes, one per stage, each with its name, years and whole-company headcount, joined by arrows.
evidence.shows: Gives the order, the years and the sizes in one view, for the reader who needs to place a stage quickly.

transition_in.carries_over: The three capacities as the reading key.
transition_in.introduces: The five stages at a glance, in a figure.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: One table gives, for each stage, the years, the headcount, the structure, the scarce capacity and the named incidents.

evidence.what: The ledger's five-stage table: 12, 50, 180, 500 and 1,100 people; product and tech 8, 28, about 113, 260, 520; structure; scarce capacity; named incidents.
evidence.shows: The lookup the acceptance criterion AC-1 is answered from.

transition_in.introduces: The same stages with structure, scarce capacity and incident.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stage 1, One table (2018–2019, 12 people): one team with no managers works because everyone hears everything, and it fails in the Founder Queue, when every pricing, design and release decision waits for Tomas Rell, the co-founder and CTO, so that judgment is the capacity that runs out.

evidence.what: Stage 1 in the ledger: 12 people, 8 in product and tech, the two founders decide everything; the Founder Queue.
evidence.shows: Shows judgment running out at one person while everything else still works.

transition_in.introduces: The first stage in detail.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stage 2, First teams (2020–2021, 50 people): four teams, two engineering managers and a first product manager take decisions off the founders, and attention runs out instead, which shows in the Two Calendars of 2021 and again in the Second Calendar of 2022.

evidence.what: Stage 2 and the append log: Web, Mobile, Integrations, Core; planners and technicians see different schedules for three weeks; the Mobile lead is replaced; eight months later a job marked complete on the phone stays open in billing exports for eleven days; the 2022 fix.
evidence.shows: Shows a rule nobody owned failing twice with different people.

transition_in.introduces: The structure that relieved the queue and what it could no longer hold.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stage 3, The hiring wave (2022–2024, 180 people): to build more than 45 engineers can, Corvane more than doubles its engineers to 95 in eighteen months; two unnamed cases follow, the even split into eleven teams and forty-one promised features shipped while renewals fall, and then every change arrives more slowly, because finished changes wait at a platform team of five, the Launch Queue of 2024, where verification and the platform team's attention have run out; what the stage leaves open is who decides that a feature is ready.

evidence.what: Median lead time for a change 4 days before the wave and 19 after; of the 19 days about two went into writing the change; 14 open launch requests at the peak; five platform engineers for eleven teams; three teams needed Platform for every launch.
evidence.shows: The figures of the introduction's puzzle, placed on the timeline: capacity was added to writing changes and the wait was at the launch.

evidence.what: Forty-one features shipped in one year of the stage, each promised to a named customer, and the renewal rate fell; the eleven teams were formed in 2023 by dividing people evenly, with no outcome stated.
evidence.shows: Tells the two unnamed cases in their stage, so the incident table classifies nothing the reader has not met.

evidence.what: The 2024 change brief led by Dario Vance: a release path the Scheduling team could run without Platform; company-wide median lead time under 7 days three quarters later.
evidence.shows: Shows the stage did not end in the queue, without retelling chapter 2.

transition_in.carries_over: Four teams and a repaired rule.
transition_in.introduces: The growth that followed and the queue it produced.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stage 4, Groups and plans (2025–2026, 500 people): four product groups with directors, a CPO, annual and quarterly planning, a career ladder and an architecture forum supply the deciding that eleven teams lacked (who says a feature is ready, which of four ways of deploying to keep), and judgment runs short again because decisions are now made far from their information, as the Nine-Week Plan and the Tuesday Reorg show.

evidence.what: In 2025 the eleven teams ran four ways of deploying, three message brokers and two identity libraries; after the launch queue was relieved the longest wait was for someone to say a feature was ready.
evidence.shows: The problems the stage 4 structures were an answer to, told here so the usage table cites nothing new.

evidence.what: Stage 4 in the ledger: quarterly planning takes nine of the quarter's thirteen weeks; a reorganization is announced without a migration plan and two teams lose their on-call rotation.
evidence.shows: Two incidents in which the people deciding did not have the information the decision needed.

transition_in.carries_over: Eleven teams with no one deciding across them.
transition_in.introduces: The coordinating structures added and what they cost.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stage 5, Scale and AI (2027–2028, about 1,100 people): after acquiring Routewise, and with coding agents in every team, writing a change becomes cheap and checking it does not, which produces the Review Wall and then the Hiring Question.

evidence.what: Merged changes per week up 2.4 times from January 2027 to January 2028 with review capacity flat; median review wait from 5 hours to 31; the 2028 plan asks whether to hire engineers at all.
evidence.shows: Shows verification and judgment as the scarce capacities once production is cheap.

transition_in.carries_over: A company coordinated by groups and plans.
transition_in.introduces: The acquisition, the agents and what ran short next.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The five stages share one shape: each structure answered the problem in front of Corvane when it was built (the fifth change, coding agents, arrived from outside), and each then stayed in place while growth made a different capacity scarce in a place the structure was not built to watch.

evidence.what: Problem answered, then where the shortage appeared: decisions waiting at a founder, answered by teams and managers, then the rules between teams; more to build than hands, answered by hiring, then the launch; nobody deciding across eleven teams, answered by groups and plans, then the distance between a decision and its facts; cheap writing from agents, then the review.
evidence.shows: States the page's claim from the five cases just told, and prepares the mapping of incidents to patterns.

transition_in.carries_over: Five stages told one by one.
transition_in.introduces: What they have in common.

sections.heading: The Incidents and the Patterns Behind Them
sections.controlling_idea: Each of Corvane's incidents is an instance of one of the twelve failure patterns, and between them the cases touch all four families.

advances_thesis.how: Classifies the incidents already told by the pattern and the designable element behind each.

transition_in.carries_over: The stages and their incidents, and the previous page's twelve patterns.
transition_in.introduces: Each incident as an instance of a pattern.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The previous page sorted twelve failure patterns into four families, one for each thing a leader can design: boundaries, interfaces, decision rights and incentives; an incident is one of those patterns with a date and a size.

evidence.what: The twelve pattern names and four families as fixed by the failure-patterns page and the style guide.
evidence.shows: Recalls the vocabulary the table uses, with each of the four elements said in a plain clause.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ten cases, the eight named incidents and two unnamed ones, each map to a primary pattern and through it to a designable element.

evidence.what: Founder Queue: the Escalation Ladder. Two Calendars and Second Calendar: the Unowned Interface. The even split of the hiring wave: the Org Chart as Architecture. Forty-one features: the Feature Factory. Launch Queue: the Overloaded Team. Nine-Week Plan: the Consensus Stall. Tuesday Reorg: the Reorg as Strategy. Review Wall: the Review Bottleneck. Hiring Question: a decision, with the Output Scoreboard as the pattern it risks.
evidence.shows: Answers the can-do outcome 'say which failure pattern each incident is an instance of'. The mapping is this page's reading and is recorded as an open question for the author.

transition_in.introduces: Corvane's cases, each matched to one.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The table gives one pattern per case although most incidents show more than one, it touches all four families (incentives only as a risk), and it leaves three patterns without a case of their own.

evidence.what: The Launch Queue is filed under the Overloaded Team and is also a queue for checks, which is the Review Bottleneck; Samir Haddad as the only engineer who understood both the scheduling engine and the mobile sync is a sign of the Hero Culture; the Platform Nobody Asked For, the Ladder as Checklist and the Hero Culture have no named incident.
evidence.shows: Keeps the table from being read as a one-to-one law and says honestly where the running example has no case.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The claim, the patterns and the company are one instrument: the claim says what can be designed, the patterns say how the design fails, and Corvane gives each failure a date and a size.
conclusion.so_what: The reader starts Part I able to say in plain words what went wrong at Corvane at each size, and ready to learn the vocabulary that explains why.

callback.to: The hiring wave the book's introduction opened with (engineers doubled, lead time from 4 days to 19), and this page's opening promise to give the company whole.
callback.how: The hiring wave is now stage 3 of five on Corvane's timeline, the stage between about 150 and 300 people, with a stage before it that explains the teams and a stage after it that explains the plans.

takeaway.content: Which of Corvane's incidents has your own organization had, and at what size?

open_questions: The mapping of incidents to failure patterns (p18) is this page's reading, made while the failure-patterns page was being written in parallel. The author should confirm it against that page, in particular: the Founder Queue as the Escalation Ladder (chapter 5 reads it as a sign of the Hero Culture), the Launch Queue as the Overloaded Team and not the Review Bottleneck, the Nine-Week Plan as the Consensus Stall, and the Hiring Question as a decision that risks the Output Scoreboard.
Parts V to XI are at outline detail in the journal spec, so the usage table assigns them a stage by subject. The table should be revisited when those parts are written.
The journal spec's Preface closing places the hiring wave 'at the 150-to-300 stage'; Corvane has 180 people at the end of stage 3. The page says both.
The thesis was written for this spec because the journal spec gives a front-matter page none; the author may want to add it to the journal spec.
